=== FILE: docs/RND_PLAN.md ===
# Pip v4: hardware R&D, operating model and plan

**Scope:** the robot's **physical design** (mechanical, electrical, industrial design, simulation, cost). The AI stack comes later.

**Concept:** [V4_CONCEPT.md](V4_CONCEPT.md). **Live numbers:** [rnd/SCORECARD.md](rnd/SCORECARD.md). **History:** [RND_LOG.md](RND_LOG.md).

**Owner's brief (2026-11-25):** Claude runs the development. Iterate over long periods, innovate, change course when the evidence says so, and don't stop at the first "done". More compute → a better robot.

---

## 1. Operating model: a continuous engineering loop

Each scheduled run (and any interactive session) does one **loop**:

1. **Sync:** `git pull`; read the scorecard, the work queue (§4), and the last few log entries.
2. **Critique.** Ask what the single highest-leverage thing is right now. Candidates:
   - the **weakest scorecard metric**
   - the **biggest unretired risk**
   - the **next thing a build needs**
   - a **better idea** that could beat the current design (look for precedent first)
3. **Do the work** with real tools:
   - build123d CAD
   - MuJoCo twin and analyses (`python -m rnd.run_all`)
   - Blender renders
   - web research with sources
   - parallel subagents for independent research, where useful
4. **Measure:** regenerate the reports and update the scorecard. **A change that makes the scorecard worse is reverted unless the log explains why it's worth it.**
5. **Decide:** update the decision table (§3). Decisions **can be reversed**; record why. Edit the queue freely: add, split, reorder or delete.
6. **Record:** commit and push to `claude/robot-dog-p2s-printer-j4esie`, and add a log entry: what, numbers before → after, files, open questions.
7. **Tell the owner:** a short summary every run. A **digest** (renders + scorecard delta + decisions taken) every ~4 runs, or after any major change. Digests **don't block**; work continues.

**Sprint mode (owner, 2026-11-27: "it's taking days when it should be hours").** Replaces the one-deliverable-per-run rule. Why it was slow: each scheduled run did *one* deliverable and then the session sat idle until the next firing, so the queue moved ≈ 2 items an hour at best, serially.
1. **Parallel tracks.** The lead splits the open queue into 3–4 tracks with **disjoint files** (e.g. arm CAD / shoulder roll / covers + pinch / electrical + software + cost) and runs one background engineer per track, each in its own git worktree. Engineers don't touch RND_PLAN, RND_LOG or the scorecard; they report, the lead merges, re-runs the affected checks on the merged tree, logs and pushes.
2. **No idle time.** The lead keeps working (integration, checks, the next wave's briefs) while engineers run; when a wave lands, the next wave starts in the same turn. Scheduled runs are now a heartbeat: if a wave is in flight they integrate whatever finished and keep going; if not, they start the next wave.
3. **Don't block on the owner.** An owner decision that is pending (e.g. D24's inline roll) is built as a params switch so the decision costs nothing either way.
4. **Checks:** each engineer runs only the checks covering its files; the lead runs `run_all --quick` + the affected heavy checks once per merged wave, full `run_all` at most once per wave of CAD changes. 4 cores: at most one heavy job (FEA, Monte Carlo) per engineer at a time.
5. Commit per finished item; one log entry per wave (≤ 5 lines per track). Don't chase the last 1 %.

**External reviews (once per day each, only after a significant batch of fixes):** Gemini 4 Neon (`rnd/external_review.py`, ≈ $1.67; the script refuses a second run within 24 h), Astra (`rnd/astra_review.py`), and a **Fable** review pass (owner, 2026-11-27) run by the lead as a review subagent after a significant merged wave; stamp file `docs/review/.fable_last` (24 h).

**The loop never "finishes".** When the queue is empty, the next run starts with a fresh critique of the whole design and writes a new queue: a stronger design, cheaper parts, easier assembly, better looks.

**Guardrails:**
- No purchases, PRs or AI-stack work.
- Every part ≤ 256 mm (P2S).
- Every actuator in a joint cartridge.
- Numbers come with sources or are marked `ESTIMATE`.
- Keep `rnd/params.py` the single source of truth.
- Only the owner decides to **buy hardware**. Milestones below end with a buy/no-buy question.

| ID | Requirement | Target | Hard limit |

| R2 | Payload per arm | 1.0 kg at 45 cm; 2.5 kg two-handed near the body | 0.6 kg at reach |
| R3 | Carry up stairs | ≤ 2 trips, pieces ≤ 10 kg with handles, split/join ≤ 30 s without tools, "carry mode" | Pieces ≤ 13 kg |
| R4 | Carpet | Low and medium pile, rugs, 15 mm thresholds, accurate position estimate | Low pile + 10 mm |
| R5 | Footprint | Base ≤ 50 cm; fits 70 cm doors with arms folded | ≤ 60 cm |
| R6 | Speed | 0.8 m/s, smooth holonomic motion | 0.5 m/s |
| R7 | Runtime | 2 h light duty | 1 h |
| R8 | Cost (excluding Pi) | ≤ $4,000 aim (was $3,300; raised for the D9 sensor pack, owner 2026-11-25) | **$5,500** (owner, 2026-11-27: raised from $5,000 to keep the inline roll and the review fixes) |
| R9 | Reusable actuators | All motors in joint cartridges | – |
| R10 | Assembly | **No hard target (owner, 2026-11-26), but reducing it is a priority.** Track first-build hands-on hours every run; reconfiguration ≤ 1 h | – |
| R11 | Looks and motion | Reads as a robot: clean shells, expressed joints, light rings, expressive head, smooth motion | – |
| R12 | Safety | Torque-limited joints, e-stop, protected 24 V, stable (tip margin ≥ 50 mm under worst static load) | – |
| R13 | Printability | Parts ≤ 256 mm, support-free where possible | – |
| R14 | **Assembly simulation** (owner, 2026-11-26) | Every part has a simulated assembly sequence: (a) each bearing slides onto its journal from a free end; (b) each part reaches its installed position along a straight insertion path without colliding with parts already installed; (c) every screw has tool access (Ø12 mm clear along its axis for ≥ 50 mm for a hex key or driver); (d) every joint cartridge can be swapped with the arm assembled. Checked by `rnd/assembly_seq.py` | 100 % of parts | all drive shafts and cartridges |
| R15 | **Spacing** (owner, 2026-11-26) | Minimum clearance between parts that are not fused or bolted together: ≥ 1.0 mm static; running clearances set by a bearing, shim or guide ≥ 0.3 mm (loop 36 refinement); ≥ 2.0 mm between other parts in relative motion over their full joint range (swept); belts ≥ 3 mm from any static part; cable bend radius ≥ 10 × OD; no belt/pulley nip reachable by a 12 mm finger probe. Checked by `rnd/spacing.py` | as stated | ≥ 0.5 mm static, ≥ 1.0 mm moving |
| R2c/R2d | **Heavy carry** (owner, 2026-11-27) | 20 lb two-handed, held close; a 20 lb laundry basket from the floor to a bed (rnd/payload_study.py, rnd/basket.py) | as stated |
| R16 | Dexterity | bench grid reachable with top-down / 45° / side / across-the-body grasps ≥ 30 / 63 / 62 / 54 % (rnd/dexterity.py) | – |
| R17 | **Pinch safety + consumer finish** (owner, 2026-11-27) | No accessible pinch or nip point anywhere on the robot: every gap between parts in relative motion is either **closed to a finger** (cover opening ≤ 8 mm, so a finger can't enter) or **≥ 25 mm over the whole joint range** (finger-crush gap; the commonly cited ISO 13854 values are finger 25 / hand 100 / arm 120 mm: confirm against the standard's table); every belt, pulley and gear enclosed; motors not visible; soft rounded shells; contact force limited in software (current-based collision detection, ≤ 140 N transient at the hands, ISO/TS 15066-style). Checked by a new rnd/pinch.py (swept gaps between link pairs over the joint ranges, a 12 mm finger probe at every cover opening) | no exposed belt or motor |

## 3. Decisions (living; reversals logged)

| # | Decision | Status | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | **Carry split: upper core / base / battery / 2 arms.** Each arm detaches at the shoulder-pitch output with a **KX-V V-band clamp** (printed 3" sanitary flanges, 3 dowels, stock quick-release clamp; loop 7: the twist collar can't carry the arm's bending) plus a blind-mate plug. Core 6.9 kg, arm 3.4 kg each, base 5.8 kg, battery 1.5 kg. Two trips: core + base, then battery + arms. *Changed* (loop 4): CAD masses put the one-piece upper at 11.9 kg (limit 10) | Changed 2026-11-25 (loop 4) | [budget](rnd/budget.md) |
| D2 | **Base: 4 × 6" omni, one wheel pointing forward, wheels at R 0.21 m, Ø500 shell.** *Reversed from 3-wheel kiwi:* kiwi tip margin was ~35–46 mm vs 66–82 mm | Changed 2026-11-25 | [twin](rnd/twin.md) |
| D2b | Cross thresholds at a **45° heading and ≤ 0.15 m/s** (loop 12 roller-level sim: 0° fails at 15 mm; 0.30 m/s reaches the GIM peak by impact, 0.15 m/s peaks ~6 N·m, 1.8×). Cap base acceleration at 1.0 m/s² with arms parked and 0.5 m/s² while manipulating. Position from optical flow + IMU + lidar | Updated (loop 12) | [threshold](rnd/threshold.md) |
| D3 | **Joint cartridges carry torque only (KX v1).** The cartridge output has a KX male face: 3 hardened balls on 3 pairs of steel dowel pins, locked by a spring-preloaded breech-lock collar (35° twist, thumb tabs, self-locking 6° ramp). It locks into a **hub that turns in the bone's own bearing pair**, and the housing is held by a **steel torque pin in a radial slot**. Sizes: KX74 (GIM6010-8), **KX56 (DM-J4310; added loop 4, saves ~45 g per socket and shrinks the wrist collar from Ø98 to Ø78)** and KX44 (STS3215). The seat doubles as an overload clutch (slip ≥ 1.16× actuator peak). Buses: 24 V CAN 1 Mbps / 12 V TTL. *Changed* from the same printed male face on both sides of every cartridge: that put arm bending (up to 12 N·m) and belt pull through printed V-grooves at 3–4× PETG yield. | Changed 2026-11-25 (loop 2) | [kx](rnd/kx.md) |
| D4 | **Arm: 0.30 + 0.28 + 0.13 m, wrist ±120°** (loop 1: ±140° folded the hand into the forearm; ±120° gives more collision-free reach). **CAD requirement:** forearm bone ends ≥ 60 mm before the wrist axis. Shoulder pitch GIM × 2.5 belt + **adjustable balancer K = 4 N·m** (τ = K·sin pitch; zero-free-length cable + 2.7 N/mm caged compression spring, pulley A on a 45–65 mm slot → K 3.6–5.2 N·m, [balancer](rnd/balancer.md)), roll GIM × **3.5**, upper-arm yaw **GIM × 2 belt** (loop 5: DM-J4310 direct was under-rated over the workspace), elbow GIM × 2, wrist pitch **DM-J4310**, wrist roll and gripper STS3215. Joints are sized on a **whole-workspace check** ([spring](rnd/spring.md)), not only the straight-arm case. *Changed* from 0.25 + 0.23, ±110°, wrist STS (reach coverage 31 % → 100 %; STS wrist was under-rated) | Changed 2026-11-25 | [arm sizing](rnd/arm_sizing.md), [twin](rnd/twin.md) |
| D4b | **Counter grasps use top-down or 45° approach, whichever is collision-free** (top-down alone reaches 62 % of counter cells, combined 100 %). Telescoping spine deferred: it would cost ~0.6 kg on a tight carry budget. Revisit if real tests show the need. | New (loop 1b) | [twin](rnd/twin.md) |
| D4d | **Bones: 1.2 mm printed shells + carbon tubes** for the upper-arm neck (Ø40×1) and the forearm link (Ø30×1), bonded into printed sockets. Stiffness, not strength, limits printed bones: the hand sagged 4.1 mm (printed only) → **1.6 mm** with CF. Precedent: Hello Robot Stretch, Kinova carbon links | New (loop 9) | [bones](rnd/bones.md) |
| D5 | **Lift: shoulder height 0.35–1.05 m. Standard GIM6010-8 cartridge on a 20T HTD 5M belt along the spine, with a spring-applied, solenoid-released ratchet pawl** (fail-safe, 0 W holding, safe carry mode). 2.1× torque margin, 3.5 s full travel, 0.55 kg. *Changed* from a NEMA23 + brake (1.25 kg, another motor type); constant-force springs rejected (they shoot up when the arms are removed; fatigue) | Changed 2026-11-25 (loop 8) | [lift](rnd/lift.md) |
| D8 | **Head fixed on top of the mast** (owner's suggestion). The torso and arms ride the lift below it. Overall height is a constant **1.29 m**. The head camera always has the high vantage (tilts 60° down for floor work, level/up for shelves; precedent: Hello Robot Stretch). The bare mast no longer pokes through the head, and 0.6 kg leaves the lift's moving mass. Reach 98 %, bimanual 4/4 and tip margin unchanged | New 2026-11-25 | [head views](rnd/img/head_camera_views.png), [render](rnd/img/robot_head_on_mast.png) |
| D9 | **Sensors favour accuracy and dexterity over cost** (owner, 2026-11-25). Sensor pack v2: joint-side absolute encoders on the 8 arm belt joints + lift (hand error 4.0 → 0.9 mm); global-shutter wrist cameras; magnetic-elastomer fingertip tactile pads (AnySkin/ReSkin principle); palm ToF; base cliff ToF; optical flow kept; 3 RP2040 CAN sensor nodes. +$276 | New (loop 15) | [accuracy](rnd/accuracy.md), [BOM](rnd/BOM_v4.md) |
| D10 | **Compute:** the owner's Pi 5 runs I/O, real-time supervision, IK and state estimation (≈ 73 % of 4 cores, ESTIMATE). The torso **reserves a bay + 19 V 3 A branch + Ethernet for a Jetson-class AI computer**, bought in the AI phase (~$249) | New (loop 17) | [compute](rnd/compute.md) |
| D11 | **Head face screen + touch panel** (owner, 2026-11-26). A bar-format LCD (~7–8", to fit the 196 × 66 mm visor; panel dimensions to verify) shows the face (the eyes are drawn on it) and status, and gives touch controls: pause/resume, home/park, joint jog, teach mode, task pick, and a STOP command. It runs on **its own ESP32-S3-class node on the CAN bus**, not on the Pi, so it still works if the Pi hangs, and the cable to the fixed head is power + one CAN pair. **The hard-wired torso e-stop stays the safety device**; the screen's STOP is a command beside it, not instead of it. ~$50–90, ~+150 g at the mast top, ~2–3 W | Adopted; design in queue item 5 | owner Q&A 2026-11-26 |
| D12 | **Cable routing: a clock-spring spiral at every joint; slim bundle.** (Loop 40: the yaw cavity is real CAD and yaw is back to ±150°, D13b.) Torsion through the short shaft bores can't absorb the ranges (cable ~±360°/m). The wrist camera becomes MIPI-CSI on an FFC through the wrist, with a CSI→USB bridge on the forearm and a slim 4-core USB (≤ Ø2.2) onward. The stiffest cable is then Ø2.2 mm (bend r 22 mm). | Adopted (loop 32); yaw cavity open | [harness.md](rnd/harness.md) |
| D13 | **Belt stage v2 (assemblability, review #1 finding 1).** Small-pulley stage: a **steel Ø12 shaft** in 2 × 6801 (12×21×5) inside thicker eccentric bushings; an **off-the-shelf aluminium HTD 5M pulley** (20T; **18T on the roll stage**, fixing the 20/18 mismatch) with set screws on a flat; a **clamp flange coupling** bolted to the printed KX74 hub on a 4 × M4 circle (≈ 5 MPa on the PETG at 12.7 N·m). The bearings slide on from the free end; the shaft drops through the walls. Big-pulley stages (pitch 60T, roll 72T, yaw 40T, elbow 40T): the printed pulley becomes a **separate part bolted to a shaft flange** (≥ 4 × M4), inserted between the walls before the shaft. Every shaft→link joint gets a key or a bolted flange. ≈ +$68 net for 9 small stages (6801s replace 61804s). | Adopted (loop 35); CAD in queue A1 | [assembly_seq.md](rnd/assembly_seq.md), review #1 |
| D14 | **Only 24 V + CAN + USB cross the shoulder.** The elbow sensor node makes 12 V (buck) and drives the TTL servo bus for the wrist roll and gripper, so the clock-spring ribbon through pitch, roll and yaw is 7.8 mm wide (2 × 20 AWG, 2 CAN pairs, slim USB). | Adopted (loop 40) | [harness.md](rnd/harness.md), [electrical.md](rnd/electrical.md) |
| D15 | **KX socket as built:** screwed retainer (3 × M3), **6 coil springs Ø4 in pockets** in a 5.5 mm hub step (installed 5 mm, 3 mm compression), pins 1 mm prouder and balls 1 mm deeper in the male face (captured past the equator + retaining compound). Replaces the print-in-place socket (its 1 mm annulus held no real spring; the pause order was wrong). KX Monte Carlo: below-peak slips 26 % → 13 %. | Adopted (loop 40; review finding 2) | [kx_mc.md](rnd/kx_mc.md), COUPONS C1/C2 |
| D16 | **Wrist roll on a bearing spindle:** the gripper bolts to a spindle in 2 × 61804 under the palm; the STS3215 drives it through a two-dog coupling (torque only). The KX44 seat would lift off at ≈ 0.6 N·m against ≈ 1.3 N·m dynamic with 1 kg. l_hand 0.15 → 0.156 m. Tools bolt to the spindle flange. The wrist-pitch KX56 stays (its bending lever is only the ≈ 40 mm hub offset). | Adopted (loop 40; review finding 5) | rnd/parts/hand.py |
| D17 | **Wheels bolt to the GIM output** (no KX on the wheels: slip risk under threshold torques, review finding 12). A 3 mm aluminium ring ties the four deck quarters. | Adopted (loop 40) | [BOM](rnd/BOM_v4.md) |

# All-inline arm study (generated by `python -m rnd.inline_study`)

Every big arm joint (shoulder pitch, shoulder roll, upper-arm yaw, elbow) driven by a geared actuator sitting on the joint
axis, as the approved inline GIM8108-36 shoulder roll (D24): no belt, pulley, stub, 6001, idler, cassette or fixed belt
centre. Variants (params ARM_MOTOR_SETS / with_arm_motors(); PIP_ARM_MOTORS=<set> for a params-level run, the default is
unchanged):
- **B0 today**: default `gim6010` set (GIM6010-8 + belt at pitch 3:1, yaw 2:1, elbow 2:1) + the inline GIM8108-36 roll.
- **B1 today + D20**: `d20` (GIM8108-8 + belt 3:1 at pitch and elbow).
- **I1 all-inline SteadyWin** (`inline`): GIM8108-36 at pitch, roll, elbow; GIM6010-48 at yaw.
- **I2a all-inline mixed** (`inline_dm`): GIM8108-36 at pitch, roll, elbow; dual-encoder DM-J4340-2EC at yaw.
- **I2b all-inline mixed** (`inline_dm8009`): as I2a with a dual-encoder DM-J8009-2EC (9:1 single stage) at the elbow.

Method. The torque, tip, basket, hug, thermal and accuracy rows re-run the existing models (rnd/spring.py, payload_study.py,
basket.py, tip.py, thermal.py network, accuracy.py constants) on each variant's params. There is **no inline CAD** for
pitch, yaw and elbow: their masses are today's CAD roll-ups (arm.masses(), shoulder.masses(), roll.masses()) minus the
belt-stage parts each variant removes (FROM CAD) plus ESTIMATE additions (MASS_LINES below; asserted against params);
envelopes are motor drawings + today's wall / cover allowances (ESTIMATE); the door stow re-measures today's stow pose
with the removed belt-stage hulls taken out and the motor cylinders added (pose not re-optimised). Back-drive force and
the collision numbers use a first-order model with cited scaling (reflected inertia J_rotor·N², back-driving
efficiency of a planetary η_b ≈ 2 − 1/η_f) and ESTIMATE rotor inertias / drag torques: **they are what the bench must
measure first**.

## Recommendation

- **Elbow for I2: DM-J8009-2EC.** The DM-J8009 is 9:1 single-stage: elbow reflected inertia 0.078 → 0.005 kg·m², back-drive 2.2 → 0.6 N at the hand, an output encoder built in, 0.10 kg lighter; the hug elbow margin 3.02 → 1.72× rated (still ≥ 1.5) for +$483 landed on the robot.
- **All-inline works on every load check** that today's default fails: the 20 lb hug 0.82× → 3.02 / 3.02 / 1.72× (B1/D20 1.84×), the basket 0.65 → 2.39 / 2.43 / 1.56; tip A10 16/16 (worst 34.8 mm) → 14/16 (28.3), 15/16 (29.6), 16/16 (30.7).
- **Cost:** robot landed, both arms' big-joint drives: B0 $1,852, B1 +$184, I1 +$727, I2a +$727, I2b +$1,210. Against the D20 path the owner already needs for R2c/R2d: I1 +$543, I2b +$1,026.
- **Mass:** arm piece 4.80 (B0) / 4.83 (B1) → 5.19 / 4.75 / 4.64 kg; the elbow actuator 0.39 → 1.00 / 0.90 kg sits on the elbow axis instead of 70 mm above it.
- **Hand-feel and impact:** back-drive at the hand stays a few newtons everywhere (it is gravity you feel when you push an unpowered arm); the hand effective mass in the reach pose goes 2.40 → 2.96 (I1) / 2.76 kg (I2b): 36:1 and 48:1 two-stage reducers put more rotor inertia in the hand than the 16:1–24:1 belt joints. The 9:1 J8009 elbow and the light 43-class J4340 yaw rotor take most of that back.
- **Accuracy:** without extra encoders 4.3 mm (B0) → 4.6 (I1) / 3.7 (I2b); with joint-side encoders 0.9 → 0.9 / 0.9 mm. The dual-encoder Damiao joints get there with no extra parts.
- **Simplicity:** drive pieces per arm 50 → 20 / 14; fasteners 108 → 67 / 63 (fewer, larger screws: 8 × M4 motor + 3 × M4 and dowels at the boss + 8 × M5 into the link per heavy joint); arm build 6.1 → 5.8 / 5.5 h; no belt to tension or measure (D26's 0–165 N fixed-centre preload spread goes away).

**Recommendation: go all-inline as I2b** (GIM8108-36 at pitch and roll, dual-encoder DM-J4340-2EC at yaw, dual-encoder DM-J8009-2EC at the elbow), as the R2c/R2d motor path instead of D20, **gated on the bench** (below), **if the owner accepts the cost: it does not save money** (+$1,026 landed against D20, +$1,210 against today; the belt-stage parts it removes are ≈ $60–70 a joint, the 36:1 and dual-encoder actuators cost $150–380 more than a GIM6010-8). It passes the hug and the basket with margin, keeps the tip gate (by 1 mm: the 1 kg pitch / elbow actuators move the COM forward, and I1 / I2a miss one or two cases), removes every belt stage on the arm (no tensioning, no fixed-centre preload spread), slims the yaw block and gives output-side encoders at yaw and elbow without extra parts. If the J8009's $470 or its lead time is a problem, I2a (GIM8108-36 elbow, +$543 against D20) is the cheaper fallback, with a stiffer elbow by hand and a tip case to recover (≈ 0.5 mm short: ballast or a planner rule). I1's GIM6010-48 yaw is the weakest choice: 48:1 two-stage (most reflected inertia at the hand of any yaw option), 20 rpm rated, no output encoder, conflicting torque listings. Keep B1 (D20) buildable as the fallback if the bench back-drive or backlash numbers come in bad.
- **Cheaper inline motors?** Not found: the GIM6010-36 (18 N·m rated, ≈ 0.57 kg) lists at $180–217 (2026-11-28 snippets), within $60 of the GIM8108-36, so the inline cost is the price of 36:1 actuators, not of the frame size. Its listing offers a 'secondary encoder' option: a dual-encoder GIM8108-36 would give I1/I2 pitch the output encoder too (seller question).

**Not covered (no inline CAD):** the inline pitch motor inside the torso next to the balancer (cord, die spring, crank: must be re-routed, the biggest packaging risk), the elbow fold clearance with a Ø105 knee, the stiffness / FEA of the new load paths (the owner is not holding us to the rigidity adders, but the hand-deflection gate R2b still applies), the R17 pinch sweep, and the 24 V speed of the Damiao parts under load.

## Hand back-drive and collision

Pushing the arm by hand: back-drive torque at the joint T = N_gear·τ_drag,motor / η_b + τ_gear (× belt ratio / η_belt + belt-stage drag for the belt joints); η_b = 2 − 1/η_f with η_f = 0.93^stages (the usual estimate for back-driving a planetary that is itself back-drivable); motor drag 0.01–0.015 N·m and gearbox breakaway 0.1 / 0.3 N·m (1 / 2 stages) are ESTIMATES. Force at the hand = T / lever (pitch and roll 0.60 m, yaw and elbow 0.43 m). Reflected inertia = J_rotor·N² (rotor inertia ESTIMATE from an 80-class actuator's published 579 g·cm², scaled by size; actuators.yaml). The 'trip' columns: an unmodelled friction band of ±50 % of T (friction of a 2-stage reducer moves with temperature and load) has to be added to the sw/collision.py threshold to keep 0 false trips; the hand force that trips the joint is then (THR + 0.5 T) / lever.

**Reading.** The chest-contact force peaks 15–17 ms after contact, about when sw/collision.py trips (14–18 ms): the first impact is set by the effective mass and the speed, not by the detector, so the reflected rotor inertia is part of the impact directly (the compliant hold only shapes what happens after). After the trip the person pushes the arm away against the back-drive force (a few N in every variant) plus whatever the compliant hold's gravity feed-forward gets wrong.

## Accuracy (hand error, joint RSS at 0.6 m)

Belt joints: rnd/accuracy.py (GIM backlash ÷ belt ratio + belt play + stretch). Inline joints: reducer backlash (actuators.yaml: GIM8108-36 / GIM6010-48 15 arcmin from listings, DM-J4340 15 and DM-J8009 10 ESTIMATE) with the motor encoder ÷ N, unless the actuator has an output-side encoder (Damiao 2EC) or a joint-side encoder is fitted (0.05° after calibration). The roll is inline in every variant.

| Variant | shoulder_pitch (no enc / enc) | shoulder_roll (no enc / enc) | upper_yaw (no enc / enc) | elbow (no enc / enc) | wrist_pitch (no enc / enc) | RSS no enc / enc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B0 | 2.1 / 0.5 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 1.9 / 0.4 | 1.9 / 0.4 | 0.1 / 0.1 | **4.3 / 0.9** |
| B1 | 2.1 / 0.5 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 1.9 / 0.4 | 1.5 / 0.4 | 0.1 / 0.1 | **4.1 / 0.9** |
| I1 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 2.0 / 0.4 | 1.9 / 0.4 | 0.1 / 0.1 | **4.6 / 0.9** |
| I2a | 2.6 / 0.5 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 0.4 / 0.4 | 1.9 / 0.4 | 0.1 / 0.1 | **4.2 / 0.9** |
| I2b | 2.6 / 0.5 | 2.6 / 0.5 | 0.4 / 0.4 | 0.4 / 0.4 | 0.1 / 0.1 | **3.7 / 0.9** |

With an output-side encoder on a joint that has backlash, the position loop closes around the backlash: expect a small limit cycle or a dead band where the gravity torque crosses zero (arm-down poses), as accuracy.md says for the roll. The Damiao 2EC actuators read the output in the actuator; a SteadyWin inline joint needs an off-axis (ring-magnet) encoder because the motor fills the axis the AS5048A uses today.

Counts: a D26 belt joint is the cartridge (can, rear cap, Al cap, NTC), the stub + key + pulley + 6001 + bushing, two eccentric bushings, the belt and the shaft-end encoder (+ the pitch idler, + the elbow cassette and seat caps); an inline joint is the actuator, a metal output adapter, a printed seat and a far-side bearing (+ an off-axis encoder for a SteadyWin). Build minutes use rnd/build_guide.py's 9 min cartridge and 15 min stage; inline heavy joint 25 min (as the roll's 35 min without the crush sleeves and stop bushes), yaw 15, encoder 7 / off-axis 10 (ESTIMATE).

## What the bench must measure to confirm it

1. **Back-drive torque** of a GIM8108-36, a DM-J4340-2EC and a DM-J8009-2EC, unpowered and in the drive's zero-torque mode: a lever + luggage scale (the Step-1 rig), breakaway and running torque, both directions, at 20 °C and after a 20-min warm-up. The model above is the mid of a 4× range; this decides the hand-feel and the collision threshold rise.
2. **Backlash** at the output of each, dial gauge on a 0.3 m lever, ± 1 N·m reversal (the 15 arcmin listing and the 10–15 arcmin ESTIMATEs): decides the no-encoder hand error and whether the encoder loop limit-cycles.
3. **Rotor inertia** (or the drive's reported inertia from a sysid chirp, sw/sysid.py) → the reflected inertia and the impact rows.
4. **Output-encoder behaviour** of the Damiao 2EC: absolute output angle over a power cycle, its noise, and whether the MIT-mode loop can use it (dual-loop) or only reports it.
5. **Torque at 24 V** and speed under load for the DM-J4340 / DM-J8009 (catalogue is 24 V rated; confirm the 36 / 100 rpm), and the GIM8108-36 output bearing's radial / tilting rating for pitch and elbow duty (≥ 612 N radial is the roll's open seller question).
6. **Collision trip** on the bench twin with the measured friction (sw/test_s1.py collision case with the new N, J and friction): trip time and the hand force at trip.



=== FILE: docs/review/inline_study_question.md ===
# Reviewer question: is an all-inline arm better for this robot?

*One page. Generated by `python -m rnd.inline_study` (numbers: docs/rnd/inline_study.md / .json).*

**The robot.** Pip v4: a 1.3 m home robot on a Ø50 cm omni base, mast lift, two 6-DOF arms (0.30 m upper arm, 0.28 m forearm, 0.156 m hand), ≈ 31 kg with removable rear ballast, 24 V. Requirements that bind here: 1 kg in one hand anywhere in the workspace; R2c 20 lb (9.07 kg) hugged two-handed; R2d a 20 lb laundry basket from the floor to a bed; tip-over reserve ≥ 30 mm in 16 braking / push cases; R17 consumer-safe (closed covers, current-based collision detection that trips in 14–18 ms, then a compliant hold); BOM limit $5,500 (today ≈ $7,500 landed, a cost-down is under way); hobby build, 3D-printed structure.

**Today.** Quasi-direct-drive SteadyWin GIM6010-8 (8:1) cartridges with an HTD 5M belt stage at shoulder pitch (3:1), upper-arm yaw (2:1) and elbow (2:1); the shoulder roll is already an inline GIM8108-36 (36:1, owner-approved). The default motors fail R2c/R2d; the planned fix (D20) puts GIM8108-8 + 3:1 belts at pitch and elbow.

**The question (owner):** would a more motor-based design help, and what would it cost? Every big joint driven by a geared actuator on its own axis, no belts / pulleys / idlers.

| | B0 today (GIM6010 belts + inline roll) | B1 today + D20 (GIM8108-8 belts at pitch + elbow) | I1 all-inline SteadyWin (8108-36 ×3, 6010-48 yaw) | I2a all-inline mixed (DM-J4340 yaw, 8108-36 elbow) | I2b all-inline mixed (DM-J4340 yaw, DM-J8009 elbow) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Big-joint drives, robot landed ($) | 1,852 | 2,036 | 2,578 | 2,578 | 3,061 |
| Arm piece (kg) | 4.80 | 4.83 | 5.19 | 4.75 | 4.64 |
| 20 lb hug, rated × (≥ 1.5) | 0.82 | 1.84 | 3.02 | 3.02 | 1.72 |
| Basket duty margin (≥ 1) | 0.65 | 1.47 | 2.39 | 2.43 | 1.56 |
| Tip worst reserve / cases ≥ 30 mm | 34.8 mm, 16/16 | 34.7 mm, 16/16 | 28.3 mm, 14/16 | 29.6 mm, 15/16 | 30.7 mm, 16/16 |
| Back-drive at the hand, N (pitch/roll/yaw/elbow; ESTIMATE) | 1.1/1.6/1.0/1.0 | 1.3/1.6/1.0/1.8 | 1.6/1.6/2.0/2.2 | 1.6/1.6/1.4/2.2 | 1.6/1.6/1.4/0.6 |
| Hand effective mass, reach pose (kg) | 2.40 | 2.61 | 2.96 | 2.92 | 2.76 |
| Hand error, no extra encoders / with (mm) | 4.3 / 0.9 | 4.1 / 0.9 | 4.6 / 0.9 | 4.2 / 0.9 | 3.7 / 0.9 |
| Drive pieces / fasteners per arm | 50 / 108 | 50 / 108 | 20 / 67 | 17 / 65 | 14 / 63 |

**Our reading.** All-inline passes every load check today's default fails and removes all belt stages; it costs +$1,026 landed against the D20 plan (I2b) and adds rotor inertia at the hand (2.40 → 2.76 kg). We propose I2b, gated on bench back-drive / backlash / rotor-inertia measurements. Back-drive and inertia figures are first-order ESTIMATES (J_rotor·N², η_b = 2 − 1/η_f, guessed drag); the inline pitch, yaw and elbow have no CAD yet.

**Please answer:**
1. Is all-inline the better architecture for this robot (home use, people nearby, 20 lb two-handed lifts, hobby build), or would you keep belts at some joints? Which, and why?
2. Are 36:1 two-stage planetaries acceptable at shoulder pitch and elbow for a robot that people push by hand and that must stop on contact (14–18 ms detection, compliant hold), or would you insist on ≤ 10:1 there? What reflected inertia / effective mass at the hand would you accept?
3. Our back-drive model (η_b = 2 − 1/η_f, motor drag × N, gearbox breakaway 0.1–0.3 N·m): reasonable, optimistic or pessimistic for these SteadyWin / Damiao units? Any measured data you know of?
4. Output-side encoders: do you trust the Damiao 2EC output encoder as the position loop's feedback with ~10–15 arcmin of backlash inside it, or only for absolute homing?
5. Packaging: an inline pitch motor in the torso shares space with a die-spring gravity balancer; a Ø105 elbow knee; a coaxial yaw under the inline roll motor. Which of these would you change first?
6. What would you change in the variant choice (actuator models, ratios, where the DM-J8009 vs GIM8108-36 goes)?



=== FILE: docs/review/fable_review_2026-11-27.md ===
# Fable design review: Pip v4, before the M1 bench-arm purchase (2026-11-27)

Scope: tree at `280715d`. I read the plan, scorecard, M1 docs and both earlier reviews, then the source (`rnd/params.py`, `rnd/parts/*.py`, the analysis modules, `sw/`). Light modules were re-run (`belts`, `accuracy`), plus three small probes of my own (driver access to the flange screws, the supervisor heartbeat, belt centre distances). No FEA or `run_all`.

**V** = verified in code or by a run. **S** = suspicion from engineering judgement, to be checked on a datasheet or a coupon.

## Verdict

1. **Buy with changes.** Buy a reduced step-1 kit now and fix six design items before printing the whole arm.
2. Step 1 is one GIM6010-8, the DM-J4310, the two STS3215, the CAN adapters, the e-stop parts, the cheap drive parts and filament. Do not take the "zero-regret" three extra GIM6010s yet: no GIM can be commanded until its CAN protocol is known.
3. The arm as drawn hangs from M3 heat-set inserts in pull-out at two joints, and the bolted cartridge's rear cap has no workable thread. Both are CAD fixes, but they come before printing.
4. The approved inline GIM8108-36 roll is the riskiest new element: a 103 N·m stall actuator on 3 mm of M4 thread, printed Ø8 stops, and backlash that the accuracy model leaves out.
5. The bench electronics are a parts list without a schematic, the supply is 10 A against the repo's own 33 A peak, and one supervisor bug would drop the arm after a detected collision.

## Critical

### C1. The whole arm hangs from M3 heat-set inserts in pull-out, twice in series (V)

- **Pitch hub to pitch tube:** `rnd/parts/shoulder.py:62, 113-131`. The hub carries the detach ferrule, so it carries the whole arm. It sits on an 8.3 mm double-D and is pulled on by 6 × M3 into inserts in the printed tube's end face (r 15.5 mm).
- **Yaw flange to yaw tube:** `rnd/parts/roll.py:549-592`. 6 × M3 countersunk into inserts in the tube end (r 16.5 mm, about 1.5 mm of wall to the Ø40 surface). Everything below the yaw hangs on them.
- **Loads:** the repo's own figure for the yaw joint is 644 N per insert with the basket, against an estimated 1.0 kN pull-out, so 1.55× on a guessed ultimate (`drive_capacity()`). The pitch hub has no capacity calculation at all. For the 19 N·m FEA case I get 200–410 N per insert static (pivot at the edge vs the centre) and 300–610 N with the ×1.5 factor. A 140 N sideways bump at the hand is 1.1–2.2 kN.
- **Not covered:** neither joint is an FEA case, and no coupon tests insert pull-out (`docs/COUPONS.md`).
- **Tightening alone can do it:** the inserts go in from the face the screw enters, so a normally tightened M3 (1 kN or more of preload) loads them in the weak direction.
- **Consequence:** the arm, or the forearm and three motors, drops off. This was the fix for Astra finding 2; it moved the problem.
- **Fix:** put the printed tubes in compression. Use through-bolts with nuts, or a hollow central tie-rod through the bore (cables still pass), or steel M4 cross-dowel nuts. Add a pull-out coupon and a capacity row for the pitch hub. Do not print the pitch or yaw shafts as drawn.

### C2. A collision "compliant hold" stops the hardware heartbeat, so the arm drops (V)

- `sw/safety.py:204` sets `healthy_cycle = True` with the comment "keep the hardware heartbeat".
- `heartbeat_ok()` (`sw/safety.py:144-145`) returns `healthy_cycle and not self.latched`, and `latched` is `["collision"]`.
- `sw/bringup.py:346` only toggles the watchdog when `heartbeat_ok()` is true.
- I ran it with a stub detector: `stop False, compliant True, heartbeat_ok False`.
- **Consequence:** 8 ms after a detected contact the watchdog opens the contactor. That is a category-0 drop onto whatever the arm just touched, the opposite of the intent.
- **Why the tests pass:** `sw/test_s1.py` has no watchdog in the rig, and `bringup.supervisor()` (`sw/bringup.py:323`) never passes `collision=`, so the bug is latent.
- **Fix:** `return self.healthy_cycle and set(self.latched) <= {"collision"}`, plus a test with `SimSafetyIO` in the loop.

### C3. The bolted cartridge (D24) cannot react motor torque as drawn, and two joints cannot be swapped (V)

- **Rear cap:** the motor bolts only to the rear cap (3 × M3). The cap is a plain 4 mm disc (`rnd/parts/cartridge_m.py:193-203`) "held by 3 radial M3 into inserts in its rim" (`:187-189`). No holes are cut in the cap, and a 4 mm rim cannot hold an M3 insert (Ø4 hole). The motor reaction therefore has no path to the sleeve.
- **Mounting face:** the design assumes the GIM6010's housing holes are on the rear face (PCD 57, marked ESTIMATE). If they are on the output face, as on many planetary actuators, the cap concept fails altogether. (S)
- **Flange inserts:** they can only be installed from the mating face, because the sleeve overhangs the back. The countersunk M4s then pull the inserts out toward the wall, which jacks the flange loose while the screw feels tight.
- **"A swap is 6 screws with the belt on"** (`cartridge_m.py:124`) is false at the elbow and at the shoulder pitch. I probed a Ø6 driver path along each screw axis:
  - Elbow: all six are blocked by the stiffened +Y housing wall. The ±75° pair also sits under the cassette's M5 spacers, 7.4 mm away (`rnd/parts/arm.py:47`). The D20 variant moved its angles for exactly this reason; the default did not.
  - Shoulder pitch: all six are blocked by the outer bracket wall.
  - Roll (belt) and yaw have driver holes (`flange_screw_access`).
- **R14 overstates:** parts (c) tool access and (d) cartridge swap are not implemented anywhere. `rnd/assembly_seq.py` checks bearing slide-on and shaft insertion only, so the scorecard's "7/7" covers less than the requirement says.
- **Fix:** give the cap an 8–10 mm skirt, or bolt the motor's front face to the step. Use captive nuts behind the flange instead of inserts (there is a 16 mm gap). Add driver holes at the elbow and pitch, and rotate the elbow bolt pattern off the posts. Implement R14 (c) and (d) as a probe like mine.

## Major

### M1. Inline GIM8108-36 roll: joints sized on impossible preloads, weak hard stops, missing backlash (V, part S)

- **Output boss** (`rnd/parts/roll.py:753`): friction is computed with 4 kN preload on M4 screws that have 3.0 mm of thread in aluminium. Line 40 of the same file rates 2.5 mm of that thread at about 1.6 kN. With a realistic 1 kN or less, the capacity is about 110 N·m against the 103 N·m stall (1.07×, not the reported 1.25×), and all of it is dowel bearing in a boss assumed to be aluminium.
- **Rear mount:** M4 × 18 through 15.5 mm of plastic into holes tapped 3.5 mm deep. The engagement is 2.5 ± 0.55 mm, so the screw either has under three threads or bottoms out. The loads are low (about 100 N per screw), but it is easy to strip a $215 motor. Use Loctited studs and nuts.
- **Hard stops:** two printed Ø8 lugs (`roll.py:305`) see 800 N at the 35 N·m software limit, about 16 MPa against the 12 MPa allowable. At stall it is 2.3 kN. The stop depends on a drive-side torque limit in a protocol nobody has read. Use steel pins.
- **Accuracy** (`rnd/accuracy.py:44`): any joint without a belt is given 0.05° "as a DM-J4310". The re-run shows the roll at 0.05° even without joint encoders. A two-stage 36:1 planetary typically has 10–20 arcmin of backlash, which is 2–3.5 mm at 0.6 m, and the roll torque crosses zero in the arm-down pose. The 0.9 mm headline excludes it. (S on the backlash figure.)
- **Ask the seller** for backlash, the output-bearing rating and which face is the output. The belt roll stays the safer M1 choice until then.

### M2. Bench power and safety electronics are not buildable or adequate as specified (V)

- **Supply:** the kit buys a 10 A CC supply and a 15 A fuse. `rnd/electrical.py:25-31` gives the arm branch 11.4 A sustained and 33.3 A peak. Astra finding 16 (15 A against 33 A) got worse, not better. A current-limit foldback on 4.7 mF browns the bus out in milliseconds, and the fuse can never blow.
- **Pre-charge against discharge:** the clamp is "forced on while the contactor is open", and pre-charge runs through 3.3 Ω while the contactor is open. As written the bus sits near 2 V and K_PRE times out. No interlock is described.
- **No schematic:** the clamp, watchdog and pre-charge exist as prose plus "comparator/reference, gate driver". This is the mandatory safety board, handling 97 A pulses, and a first-time builder would be designing it.
- **Watchdog margin:** an 8 ms hardware watchdog on a Python loop on non-real-time Linux over USB-CAN will trip on ordinary jitter, and each trip is a category-0 drop. (S) The 50 ms budget leaves room for about 25 ms.
- **Fix:** after the 1 A first power-up, use a 24 V supply of 25 A or more. Draw and review a schematic. Gate the forced discharge as a one-shot on the opening edge. Widen the watchdog.

### M3. Joint encoders and the wrist servos have no mount and no software (V)

- No encoder, magnet or board pocket exists in any arm CAD file (a search of `rnd/parts/*.py` finds only the tactile pad).
- The shaft bores an on-axis AS5048A needs are taken by cables, the balancer crank and the hub.
- `sw/bringup.py:31` says the RP2040 nodes and the STS3215 bus through the elbow node are not covered. There is no node firmware in the tree.
- **Consequence:** M1's stated proofs ("hand accuracy with the joint encoders ≤ 1 mm", "the fin-ray grasp") cannot run, and the wrist roll and gripper cannot move through the planned path.
- **Fix:** design the mounts (off-axis ring magnets or through-bore sensors) and write the node firmware first, or drive the servos from the USB-TTL adapter for M1 and drop the accuracy claim.

### M4. The GIM protocol gates everything; three driver types in one arm (S)

- `sw/drivers/gim.py` is all TODO. The safety concept (total-torque bound, torque feedback for collision detection, CAN timeout, a flash torque limit) assumes an MIT-style impedance mode on the SDC104, the SDC303 and the GIM8108-8's driver.
- If one of them offers only position or velocity modes, `sw/safety.py` does not apply to that joint.
- **Fix:** buy one GIM6010-8, prove enable, impedance, limit and timeout on it, then buy the rest.

### M5. Belt adjusters are used up at nominal; drive joints rely on friction (V geometry, S capacities)

- I solved the centre distance for the stock belts against the ±1.0 mm eccentric (`rnd/parts/belt_stage.py:108`):

| Stage | Stock belt | Centre in CAD | Centre needed | Adjuster used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yaw | 315 mm | 80.00 (`roll.py:57`) | 80.94 | 94 % |
| Elbow | 295 mm | 70.00 | 70.71 | 71 % |
| Pitch | 355 mm | 70.00 | 70.29 | 29 % |

- The yaw stage has nothing left for tension, print tolerance or belt tolerance. Astra finding 11 is not closed. Fix: set the centres to 80.9 and 70.7.
- Torque passes through an aluminium pulley with set screws on a Ø12 flat, and through a clamp hub on a plain shaft. At the 11 N·m peak that is 1.8 kN at the shaft surface, reversing. Generic D40 Oldham couplings are catalogued at about 9–10 N·m. Fix: flats on both seats, retaining compound, and a datasheet rating of at least 12 N·m.

### M6. Hold A is not "motors only" (V)

- The buy-now list has 3 × D40 Oldham couplings for pitch, yaw and elbow. The D20 variant needs Ø50 couplings at pitch and elbow (`cartridge_m.py:27-28`). The M1 doc says "no other bought part changes".
- With 22 N·m at the 20T pulley, the repo's own check gives 1382 N peak pull and 2.8× ultimate (flagged ⚠️ by `PIP_ARM_MOTORS=d20 python -m rnd.belts`).
- That pull is about 0.7 kN on each 6801 (C0 about 1.0 kN), and 3.7 kN at the Ø12 clamp and set screws.
- **Fix:** D20 needs a Ø15 keyed stage and a 25 mm or steel-cord belt. Treat it as a redesign.

### M7. Thermal and torque margins are optimistic (V assumptions)

- `rnd/thermal.py:23-30`: rated torque is taken to give 60 K in still air, and the enclosure adds a flat 10 K. The motors sit in closed 3 mm ASA sleeves with a plastic cap and plastic couplings, so there is no conduction path. R17 then adds covers.
- The rated margin is 1.55× only at the 95th percentile. At the worst pose it is 1.17× (pitch) and 1.36× (yaw, elbow).
- The scorecard's planar "2.21×" row scales every mass inward with reach (`rnd/arm_sizing.py:24-26`), which is an artefact.
- Expect derating. Fit thermistors and a metal rear cap from day 1; neither is in the kit.

### M8. Balancer pulleys overloaded (S)

- The moving pulley carries the spring force, 634–748 N, on a U604 (a 604 bearing, C0 about 0.35 kN).
- The Ø11 sheave on 2 mm UHMWPE cord is a D/d of 5.5.
- **Fix:** use 608- or 625-class grooved pulleys (`rnd/balancer.py:31`).

## Minor

- **R17 is not on the scorecard** although `pinch.md` reports 62 nip fails and 31 exposed drive parts. The bench arm is not finger-safe: keep the keep-out zone.
- **`M1_READINESS.md` is stale in places:** "CAD assumes Ø100 × 60 and 6 × M4", "owner OK pending". `stiffness.md` (8.5 mm), the scorecard (11.0) and the readiness doc (10.9) disagree.
- **Custom metal parts are not in the kit:** the balancer crank (Ø44 × 4 aluminium with a pressed Ø6 pin) and a stand. The 7075 roll adapter is listed, at an estimated $30.
- **Six countersunk screws plus a centring lip** over-constrain the flange. Use button heads.
- **The regen and branch tables still assume four GIM6010s** on the roll row.
- **DM-J4310 `t_max` as a torque limit** is the MIT mapping range. The code marks it VERIFY, which is right.

## Earlier reviews: what really closed

- **Closed:** trapped bearings and split pulleys (D13, D19), the balancer (real spring, sign fixed), clock-spring packing, regen energy sizing, supervisor v2 torque bound, the roll teeth.
- **Not closed:**
  - Astra 2: now C1.
  - Astra 11: the yaw belt, M5.
  - Astra 14: R14 is nominal only, now C3.
  - Astra 16 and 18: now M2.
  - Astra 9 and Gemini 7: margins and thermal, M7.
  - Astra 22: the commissioning items.

## What's solid

- **The process.** ESTIMATE tags, holds on unconfirmed motors, seller questions, coupons before bulk buying, and a current-limited first power-up with a catch and tether.
- **The drive train for the GIM6010 set.** Steel shafts, bought pulleys, sustained belt pull 1.5–1.8× on a conservative 312 N rating, one-piece shaft-pulleys, and the bearing slide-on check.
- **The software core.** The MIT codec matches Damiao's layout. The supervisor's total-torque bound, latched faults, and stale or NaN feedback checks are sound. The momentum-observer math is correct.
- **Honest negatives.** The P2 FEA rerun, R2b reported as failing, wrist roll limited to ±120°, and R17 measured rather than assumed.
- **Buy without regret:** the DM-J4310, the STS3215s, one GIM6010-8, bearings, belts, CAN adapters, the contactor and mushrooms, and filament.



=== FILE: docs/review/neon_2026-11-27/gemini4neon_review.md ===
### Design Review Findings

1. **Safety board netlist has three circuit-level bugs: destructive inductive flyback on the clamp, contactor chatter on bus sag, and an unblowable main fuse**
   * **Severity:** Critical
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/electrical.md` (*A5 v2: Safety board*, *Bench supply*, *Regen clamp*). `R1–R3` are **3 × Vishay RH-50 0.56 Ω** (wirewound) switched at **49 A each (146 A total)** by `Q1–Q3` (`IRFB7530`, 60 V) via a fast `UCC27524` gate driver and `TLV3702` comparator (0.4 V hysteresis) with no flyback diodes. `Q4` (K1 coil) is gated by `LATCH ∧ WD_OK ∧ PRE_OK` (`PRE_OK`: `VBUS ≥ VIN − 3 V`). `U6` (`SN74LVC1G123`) triggers on `B = AUX_OK falling edge`. Main fuse `F1` is **40 A ATO** on the `SE-1000-24` (**41.7 A** CC limit).
   * **Why it matters physically:**
     * *Inductive flyback & oscillation:* Standard Vishay **RH-50** resistors are inductive wirewound (the non-inductive part is **NH-50**), with ~2–5 µH plus lead inductance. Switching 49 A off in ~100 ns produces $V = L\frac{di}{dt} > 500\text{ V}$, immediately avalanching and shorting the 60 V `IRFB7530`s. Furthermore, on the 7.1 mF bench bus (11.8 mF robot), 146 A drops `VBUS` by 0.4 V in **19 µs** (32 µs robot), faster than the nanopower `TLV3702`'s ~36–60 µs propagation delay—causing severe undershoot and ~10 kHz hard-switched banging.
     * *Contactor chatter:* Because `PRE_OK` stays in K1's hold equation after K1 closes, any transient bus sag > 3 V (drive surge or supply current-limit foldback) opens K1 while `LATCH` stays high, immediately re-closing K2 (`LATCH ∧ ¬AUX`) and cycling K1/K2 until contacts weld or `R3` burns.
     * *Pinout & fuse errors:* On `SN74LVC1G123`, pin `B` is rising-edge triggered (`Ā` is falling-edge). A 40 A ATO fuse carries 104% rated current (41.7 A) indefinitely and will never clear a fault fed by the SE-1000-24.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Replace `RH-50` with **NH-50** non-inductive resistors and add a fast 60 V / 60 A freewheeling Schottky across each resistor; replace `TLV3702` with a fast comparator (e.g. `TLV3202`, < 100 ns) and widen clamp hysteresis to ~0.8 V or add a minimum-on-time monostable; latch K1's `PRE_OK` condition with `AUX` (`Q4 = LATCH ∧ WD_OK ∧ (PRE_OK ∨ AUX)`) and clear `LATCH` if `AUX` drops unexpectedly after closing; move `U6` trigger to `Ā`; draw a full KiCad schematic and simulate in LTspice/SPICE before ordering parts; size `F1` to 30 A (or rely on the SE-1000-24 CC limit + branch fuses, and verify fuse clearing on the battery pack where short-circuit current is > 200 A).
   * **Confidence:** 95%

---

2. **D24 bolted cartridges regressed to 2–3 asymmetrically clustered flange ears, while BOM/M1 still specify failed D40 Oldhams and an unanalyzed printed ASA Oldham tongue**
   * **Severity:** Critical
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/integration.md` (table: `lift_can` 2/2, `l_sh_can` 3/3, `l_roll_yaw_can` 2/2, `l_arm_e_can` 4/4, despite header text requiring "at least 5 of 6"); `docs/rnd/assembly_seq.md` (*Every fastener*: yaw screws at **+145° / −145°**, a 70° arc; lift at **+140° / −140°**, an 80° arc; pitch at **+40° / −30° / −70°**, a 110° arc); `docs/rnd/belts.md` (D40 POM disc **0.86× ❌**, plain Ø12 clamp hub **0.65× ❌**); `docs/rnd/BOM_v4.md` & `docs/M1_BENCH_ARM.md` (still buying D40 Oldhams, plain Ø12 h6 rod, set-screw 20T pulleys, and 6 × M4 csk screws/inserts); `docs/rnd/assembly.md` (`cartridge M Oldham adapter (D24)`, 8 mm printed ASA).
   * **Why it matters physically:** Dropping from 6 symmetric screws to **2 screws spanning 70° on one side of the circle** (yaw, lift) leaves 290° of the motor flange unclamped. Under 11 N·m peak torque plus the overhanging ~0.6 kg motor mass (~60 mm cantilever) and Oldham radial reaction forces, the flange rocks away from the wall on the unsupported side, prying the 2 printed ASA ears in bending/shear. Separately, `belts.md` proved a machined **POM** D40 disc fails at 9.5 N·m (0.86×); a **3D-printed ASA** tongue adapter bolted to the warm motor output at the same radius has lower shear/bearing strength and worse creep, yet has zero calculation or FEA, while BOM/M1 still buy the failing D40 / unkeyed Ø12 hardware.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Restore ≥ 4 well-distributed flange bolts (≥ 180° span, or 3 at 120°) by routing driver access holes through the opposite wall/bracket; replace the printed ASA Oldham tongue with a **bought machined aluminium motor-side hub** bolted to the GIM output (using the D50 Oldham + 4×4 keyed Ø12 shaft/pulley that `belts.md` already proved necessary); sync `BOM_v4.md`, `M1_BENCH_ARM.md`, `BUILD_v4.md`, and `integration.md` to the D50 keyed architecture and enforce the ≥ 4-screw symmetry check in `integration.py`.
   * **Confidence:** 95%

---

3. **C1 tie-rod joints will lose essentially 100% of preload to PETG creep, and the 4 mm 7075-T6 crank thread strength is overestimated**
   * **Severity:** Critical
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/joints.md` (*Hardware*, *C1*). Yaw tie: 6 × M3×40 (12.9) at 1.0 kN → **9.5 MPa** continuous compression on printed PETG; pitch tie: 4 × M4×78.8 (10.9) at 1.5 kN → **8.8 MPa** continuous compression; both assume "Preload loss by creep × 0.75 (ESTIMATE)". Pitch studs thread **4 mm** through the 7075-T6 crank, credited with **11.6 kN** strip strength against **6.14 kN** stall load.
   * **Why it matters physically:** Steel bolts are far stiffer than printed PETG. At 1.0 kN over ~32–40 mm clamped length, an M3 bolt ($A_s = 5.03\text{ mm}^2$) stretches only **30–38 µm**; an M4 stud ($A_s = 8.78\text{ mm}^2$) at 1.5 kN over ~70 mm stretches **57 µm**. Under **8.8–9.5 MPa** static compression—especially near warm motors at 40–50 °C—FDM PETG typically experiences **0.2%–1.0% creep strain** over days to weeks, shortening a 40–75 mm tube by **80–750 µm**. That wipes out 100% of bolt preload (not 25%). Once unpreloaded, both joints gap under ordinary service loads, chewing up the printed hex/double-D torque fits and putting the M3/M4 bolts into cyclic bending fatigue. In addition, 4 mm tapped M4 (1.0D) minus thread chamfers leaves ~3.0–3.3 mm of effective engagement (~7–8 kN strip in 7075-T6, not 11.6 kN), giving ~1.15–1.3× margin at stall rather than 1.9×.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Put **stacked Belleville (disc) spring washers** (e.g., DIN 2093, ≥ 0.4–0.6 mm elastic travel at 1.0–1.5 kN) under every tie-rod nut/head so 0.2 mm of PETG creep drops preload by < 30% instead of 100%, OR run the tie-rods through **internal aluminium/steel crush sleeves** (or switch the short pitch/yaw tubes to machined 6061 tubes bonded/keyed to printed pulleys). Thicken the 7075 crank to ≥ 6.5 mm (1.6D engagement) or use a through-nut/flanged boss. Run the 40 °C creep coupon for 168 h *with torque-to-re-tighten / bolt-tension measurement* before committing to un-sprung polymer clamping.
   * **Confidence:** 90%

---

4. **Severe tip-over instability (10/16 A10 cases fail up to −102 mm), and D18 anti-tip casters physically conflict with R4 thresholds and R5 doors**
   * **Severity:** Critical
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/SCORECARD.md` (A10: worst ZMP **−102 mm**, only **6/16 cases ≥ 30 mm**; mass roll-up: base 6.31 kg + battery 1.10 kg = 7.41 kg vs upper core 8.50 kg + two arms 9.36 kg = **17.86 kg**, i.e., **71% of the 25.26 kg robot** is above the base); `rnd/params.py` (`wheel_radius_pos = 0.21` → 148 mm inscribed diamond radius; `clearance = 0.025`); `docs/RND_PLAN.md` (D2b: cross 15 mm thresholds at **45° heading**; R5: **70 cm doors** vs Ø50 cm base; D18: spring-loaded ball transfer casters, **5 N preload, 5 mm stroke**).
   * **Why it matters physically:** A 1.29 m tall robot with 71% of its mass high up on a 148 mm support radius is intrinsically top-heavy; adding a 9.1 kg (20 lb) laundry basket or a 30 N household bump guarantees tip-over outside narrow static poses. The D18 anti-tip ball-transfer units cannot solve this without breaking R4: if mounted 5 mm above the floor, they snag on 15 mm thresholds and drag in medium-pile carpet; if mounted 18 mm up to clear thresholds, the base must pitch **4.5°** before touchdown, shifting the 18 kg upper CG outward by **~70 mm** and dynamically slamming the tiny ball transfer into the floor. Similarly, approaching a 15 mm doorway threshold at a mandatory 45° heading (`D2b`) while leaving only 10 cm clearance per side in a 70 cm doorway is operationally brittle, and small passive omni rollers dig into medium-pile carpet and slip asymmetrically.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Move heavy mass down (move the 1.1 kg battery, power distribution, contactor/clamp, and optional steel/lead ballast—3–5 kg—to the bottom of the base; keep total base ≤ 10 kg by splitting the battery or adding a removable 3 kg ballast plate for stairs) and/or widen the wheelbase to a **520–560 mm** octagon or **retractable/trailing outrigger or 4-wheel swerve/diff-drive + large-caster base** (a differential-drive base with 6" main wheels + large spring-damped front/rear casters handles thresholds at 0°, carpets far better than omni rollers, and eliminates the 45°-diamond weakness, at the cost of pure sideways strafing). Simulate D18 caster ground clearance vs 15 mm threshold and carpet sinkage in MuJoCo—not just quasi-static flat-floor ZMP.
   * **Confidence:** 90%

---

5. **R17 pinch safety is hidden off the scorecard and relies on an unsafe software "person near" soft-limit plus a hazardous Category-0 free-fall drop**
   * **Severity:** Critical
   * **Evidence:** `docs/review/fable_review_2026-11-27.md` (*Minor*: `pinch.md` shows **62 nip fails and 31 exposed drive parts**; R17 omitted from `SCORECARD.md`); `docs/RND_PLAN.md` (D25: inboard shoulder-roll wedge **135 → 2 mm** over −15…+100° mitigated by a "software soft limit when people are near", roll ≥ +15°); `docs/rnd/electrical.md` (*Category-0 drop protection*: arm drops releasing **14–23 J**; gripper back-drives and drops payload; GIM8108-36 reflected inertia **2.17 kg·m²**).
   * **Why it matters physically:**
     * *Unacceptable software guarding:* A 103 N·m stall actuator (GIM8108-36) closing a 135 → 2 mm scissor wedge against the torso generates > 1,000 N of crushing force. Relying on non-safety-rated vision ("people are near") fails the instant a child approaches from behind or perception misses a hand—and worse, hitting e-stop removes torque so **gravity drops the arm right back through roll = +15° to −15°**, closing the exact pinch wedge it was supposed to prevent!
     * *Category-0 drop & impact inertia:* Dropping a 6 kg arm + 1–4.5 kg load onto whatever person/object triggered a stop (and dropping hot/breakable objects out of a back-drivable gripper) creates secondary injury. Meanwhile, the 36:1 inline roll's high reflected inertia (2.17 kg·m²) delivers a stiff transient impact spike before a 14–18 ms software collision observer can react.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Put R17 pinch/exposed counts on `SCORECARD.md` as a hard gate; eliminate the shoulder-roll scissor mechanically by adding a **fixed hard stop at roll ≥ +10–15°** (accepting a small adduction trade) OR shaping the torso shoulder recess/conical shroud so the gap stays **≥ 25 mm** across the full mechanical range (or filled by a compliant closed-cell foam gusset); replace bare Category-0 free-fall on the full robot with either **hardware dynamic braking** (shorting motor phases via fail-safe NC relay/resistor bank on e-stop so the arm sinks slowly at < 0.2 m/s instead of free-falling) or a safety-rated SS1 delay relay.
   * **Confidence:** 95%

---

6. **Inline GIM8108-36 shoulder roll: dowel bearing stress inflated to 240 MPa, rear mount reverted to a creeping shimmed-PETG stack, and hyperstatic rear 61806 bearing**
   * **Severity:** Major
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/joints.md` (*M1*) vs `docs/rnd/roll_inline.md` vs `docs/M1_BENCH_ARM.md` (*Hold B*). Output boss bearing allowable jumped from **150 MPa** (`roll_inline.md`, giving 103 N·m = 1.00× stall) to **240 MPa** (`joints.md`, giving 164 N·m = 1.60× stall) assuming 3 × Ø4 m6 dowels 4 mm deep in an unverified boss material. Rear mount in `M1_BENCH_ARM.md` promises Loctited studs + nuts, but `joints.md` and `BOM_v4.md` reverted to **8 × M4×18 screws** + 0.3 mm hand-picked shims through **13.9 mm of PETG** at **0.5 kN** preload into 3.5 mm blind housing threads. Two Ø10 hard-stop pins sit at **r = 43 mm** (right on the r = 42 mm rear bolt circle!) carrying **2,393 N** at stall in PETG. A rear **61806** bearing sits on a printed PETG stub 68 mm behind the motor's internal output bearing.
   * **Why it matters physically:**
     * *Dowel load sharing:* Unless the GIM8108-36 output boss has CNC-jig-bored H7 dowel holes true to ±0.01 mm (unlikely on a $240 planetary actuator; not yet confirmed by the seller), **one dowel takes most of the load first**, dropping bearing capacity to ~55 N·m (half of 103 N·m stall).
     * *Rear screw creep:* At 0.5 kN over 14.7 mm grip, an M4 screw stretches only **4 µm**; trivial PETG creep drops preload to zero, eliminating the claimed 38 N·m friction and slamming the screws against 3.0 mm of blind aluminium thread.
     * *Over-constrained bearing pair:* Bridging the motor's stiff internal output bearing with an external 61806 mounted on a printed PETG stub via a printed PETG rear arm (over a 100+ mm FDM tolerance loop) creates a hyperstatic spindle. A 0.3 mm FDM alignment error either **binds the bearings** (adding unpredictable friction that blinds the collision observer) or leaves the 61806 unloaded so the motor's internal bearing carries the full 19–184 N·m tilting moment anyway.
     * *Stop pin edge distance:* Two Ø10 pins at r = 43 mm in a Ø96–100 mm housing leave minimal radial PETG wall and crowd the PCD 84 (r = 42 mm) rear screws; 2.4 kN stall load will cleave printed PETG.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Do not approve Hold B until the seller drawing confirms output boss material, hole tolerances/depths, and internal bearing **tilting moment rating** (if the GIM8108-36 uses a crossed-roller bearing rated ≥ 40–60 N·m, **delete the hyperstatic rear 61806 bearing and rear arm entirely**—saving mass, alignment pain, and cost!). Switch rear mount to true **Loctited studs + nuts + Belleville washers** (or an aluminium backing plate). Tie the Ø10 hard-stop pins into a **laser-cut steel/aluminium stop plate** sandwiched under the rear mount, not bare PETG.
   * **Confidence:** 85%

9. **FEA strength margins rely on locking P1 tets and 99.5th-percentile truncation on isotropic 1.8 GPa/12 MPa PETG, while the 5.1 mm stiffness chain omits major compliance sources**
   * **Severity:** Major
   * **Evidence:** `docs/rnd/fea.md` (all 13 strength checks are **P1 tets**, 99.5th pct; pitch tie fault **3.9 MPa 99.5th vs 19.6 MPa max**, service **2.6 vs 14.4 MPa max**); `docs/rnd/stiffness.md` (P2/P1 rotation ratio **1.56–4.08×**, P2 99.5th stress up to **2.75× P1**; reports **5.1 mm raw / 1.0 mm after 80% gravity model**); `docs/rnd/SCORECARD.md` (mast sway **1.5 mm** static).
   * **Why it matters physically:**
     * *Strength:* `stiffness.md` proved P1 tets underpredict bending deformation by up to 4.08× and stress by up to 2.75×, yet `fea.md` still reports P1 stress margins! Discarding the top 0.5% of a 44k–138k mesh throws away **220–690 elements**—erasing real stress concentrations around bolt holes and double-D roots (where pitch service already hits 14.4 MPa > 12 MPa). Moreover, FDM PETG with infill (not 100% solid) at 40–50 °C has effective $E \approx 0.9\text{–}1.3\text{ GPa}$ and a cyclic Z-layer fatigue endurance limit of **~5–7 MPa**, not 12 MPa.

Real uncompensated hand sag + backlash will likely be **10–15 mm**, and non-repeatable friction/backlash/creep means a static gravity model cannot reliably remove 80% of it.
   * **Concrete fix or test:** Re-run all 13 `fea.md` cases with **P2 elements**, report **max principal tension aligned with the actual print Z-axis** separately from in-plane stress, use a 99.9th-percentile or local-mesh-convergence check (not 99.5th), and drop the cyclic Z-layer allowable to **6–8 MPa**. Add V-band, carriage/mast, and roll-backlash terms to `stiffness.py`, and measure real end-effector deflection + hysteresis on the Step-2 bench arm with a dial indicator.

### The 5 Assumptions Most Likely Wrong

1. **"Printed PETG under 8.8–9.5 MPa static tie-rod compression retains 75% of bolt preload over its life" (`docs/rnd/joints.md`).** With only 30–57 µm of elastic bolt stretch on M3×40 / M4×78.8 fasteners, even 0.15%–0.3% viscoelastic creep (typical for PETG at 9 MPa and 40 °C) drops preload to **0%**, not 75%.
2. **"The GIM6010-8 / GIM8108-36 / GIM8108-8 all expose a clean, low-latency MIT impedance mode with flash-persistent torque limits and hardware CAN timeout" (`docs/M1_READINESS.md`, `docs/sw/sim2real_bench.md`).** Mixing three different SteadyWin driver generations (SDC104, SDC303, unknown 8108-8) on one arm makes it very likely at least one lacks MIT impedance mode, flash torque clamping, or a sub-50 ms CAN timeout—breaking the software safety argument.
3. **"A finned aluminium rear cap on the GIM6010-8 yields `h_o = 12 W/m²K` and restores 1.00× continuous torque inside R17 covers" (`docs/rnd/thermal.md`).** The rear face houses the driver PCB/connectors (blocking stator conduction), and natural convection inside a vented ≤ 8 mm consumer shroud is realistically **3–5 W/m²K**, leaving motors derated to ~0.65–0.75× rated.
4. **"An isotropic 1.8 GPa / 12 MPa PETG FEA model and an 80% gravity-compensation model yield 1.0 mm hand deflection" (`docs/rnd/fea.md`, `docs/rnd/stiffness.md`).** Printed infill + warm ambient drops effective modulus to ~1.0–1.3 GPa, cyclic Z-layer fatigue is ~5–7 MPa, and unmodeled V-band/carriage/15-arcmin-backlash compliance adds 5–8 mm of largely non-repeatable error that static gravity modeling cannot cancel.
5. **"A 500 Hz Python control loop on a Raspberry Pi 5 running 5 USB-CAN adapters, 3 cameras, and lidar stays below half a 25 ms (±20% = 20 ms) hardware watchdog" (`docs/rnd/electrical.md`).** Non-RT Python GC + USB3 camera/CAN interrupt bursts at ~73% CPU load will almost certainly produce > 20 ms stalls, causing frequent Category-0 drops unless the real-time loop moves to C/C++/Rust on an isolated `PREEMPT_RT` core.

---

### The 5 Strongest Aspects of the Design

1. **Disciplined, falsifiable parametric verification pipeline (`rnd/params.py` → CAD, MuJoCo twin, Monte Carlo, `assembly_seq.py`, `swept.py`, `pinch.py`).** Having automated geometry checks that catch bearing slide-on traps, internal clashes, swept clearances, and tool-driver access cones—and transparently tagging unverified values as `ESTIMATE`—is dramatically better than standard hobby/prototype robotics practice.
2. **Splitting M1 into a gated Step 1 / Step 2 purchase plan with explicit quantitative exit criteria (`docs/M1_BENCH_ARM.md`, `docs/M1_READINESS.md`).** Refusing to buy 4+ actuators before discovering the SDC104 CAN protocol, validating the safety board on a dummy load, and running a 2-hour hot/cold `sw/soak.py` sysid drift test saves thousands of dollars in sunk-cost mistakes.
3. **Architecture of the shoulder gravity balancer (`D4`, `A9`, `rnd/spring.py`) and lift ratchet pawl (`D5`, `A15`).** Canceling 40% of pitch self-weight with a real ISO 10243 die spring + 2:1 UHMWPE tackle cuts continuous motor heating substantially, and a fail-safe spring-applied steel ratchet pawl (`0 W` holding, safe during carry/e-stop) is the right mechanical solution for a vertical lift.
4. **Realistic bus-fault and sysid rehearsal framework (`docs/sw/sim2real_bench.md`, `sw/bus_sim.py`, `sw/sysid.py`).** Modeling jitter, packet loss, CRC errors, bus-off, and post-CRC payload corruption caught real latent bugs (stale queued replies, register-read watchdog starvation, stiction bias in static $K_t$ estimation) before touching hardware.
5. **Willingness to reverse flawed mechanical architectures based on evidence (`D13`, `D16`, `D17`, `D19`, `D24`, `C1`).** Abandoning print-in-place KX sockets, isolating wrist-roll loads onto a dedicated 2×61804 bearing spindle, moving small pulleys onto steel Ø12 shafts, bolting wheel hubs directly, and replacing pull-out M3 inserts with metal-threaded tie-rods shows strong engineering maturity—even though several of those recent fixes still need one final tightening pass to close cleanly.


=== FILE: docs/rnd/joints.md ===
# Arm structural joints: C1 tie-rod joints + M1 inline roll (generated by `python -m rnd.joints`)

C1: the pitch hub → pitch tube and the yaw flange → yaw tube joints were 6 × M3 into heat-set inserts in pull-out. Both
are now **tie-rod joints**: steel or aluminium threads only, the printed tube and hub clamped in compression between
metal parts (rnd/parts/shoulder.py HUB_TIE, rnd/parts/roll.py YAW_TIE). M1: the inline GIM8108-36 output boss, its rear
screws and its hard stops.

Loads at each joint interface come from the twin (rnd/twin.py, CAD masses) as the full wrench of everything outboard of
the interface: **pull-off** N (along the joint axis, outboard), **bending** M (the prying moment, perpendicular to the
axis), **torsion** T (about the axis, carried by the double-D / hex form fit, not by the tie).
- **Basket** (R2d): the rnd/basket.py targets with the D20 motors and 4.54 kg per hand; every collision-free IK solution
  is kept (an upper bound on the planner's pick), × 1.5 dynamic.
- **Hug** (R2c, rnd/payload_study.py case B): upper arm hanging, forearm horizontal, 4.54 kg 0.30 m out along the
  forearm, yaw 0/±45°, × 1.5 dynamic.
- **Bump**: 140 N at the grasp point (R17 transient contact limit) in ±X/±Y/±Z, arm hanging / forward / abducted /
  elbow 90°, plus the arm's weight. A fault/abuse load: checked against ultimate, the joint may gap.
- **Stall**: each of pitch, roll and elbow at its peak (D20 set, the worse one) driving the hand into a rigid block (the
  block force = stall torque / lever, in the joint's direction of motion), same poses. Fault load, as the bump.

Joint model (clamp()): a rigid metal end plate (crank/clamp ring, aluminium flange) on the printed contact annulus,
which is a compression-only elastic foundation (E 1.8 GPa over the printed stack length), with the bolts/tie as springs
holding the preload. It gives the moment at which the interface starts to gap, and the bolt force and peak printed
contact stress under each case. Criteria: service (basket, hug) no gap and contact ≤ 12 MPa; fault (bump, stall) bolt
≤ proof load, thread strip ≥ 1.5 × the bolt force, contact ≤ 40 MPa (PETG compressive yield ≈ 55–60 MPa, ESTIMATE;
compression closes the layers, so the across-layer 12 MPa does not apply).

Preload over life (Neon review 2026-11-27, finding 3 / assumption 1): the flat "× 0.75 for creep" is replaced by a
creep model (life_preload(): effective modulus, creep coefficient φ bounded from printed-PETG data, + embedding + a
cold day). With it, the wave-3 joints (print as the clamped member) keep ≈ 30 % of their preload, and the yaw tie
gaps under the basket wrench. Disc springs in series (the review's fix) keep more preload but soften the bolts, whose
stiffness carried the bending (disc_alternative()): not enough. So each C1 bolt now runs in steel crush sleeves
(SleeveClamp: bolt ↔ sleeve metal stack, the print sandwiched with a light squeeze): the preload only loses its
embedding, the no-gap moment is the metal stack's, and the service rows are checked at that life preload with the
print's squeeze crept away; the fault rows at the fresh and the life preload. M1 rows (inline
GIM8108-36): output dowels with load sharing, the metal rear clamp (plate + sleeves), the two-bearing roll support
(61806 + the motor's output bearing: reactions per load case from the twin, misalignment preload), the hard stops.

## Hardware

- **Pitch hub ↔ pitch tube** (rnd/parts/shoulder.py HUB_TIE): 4 × M4 class 10.9 studs (DIN 976-1, cut to 78.8 mm) on r 15.5 at 45° + k·90°, Loctite 270 into the 7075-T6 balancer crank (tapped through 4 mm, stud end flush with its inboard face), each in two steel crush sleeves Ø7.0 / Ø4.3 (turned 42CrMo4+QT; one through the tube wall r 11–20, one through the hub, butting at the hub ↔ tube face, each 0.05 mm shorter than its print), M4 nuts (ISO 4032 class 8, Loctite 243) on a 6061 clamp ring r 11–21 × 2 in a 5.7 mm recess of the detach face; 1.5 kN each (≈ 1.3 N·m, ESTIMATE). Assembly: tube into the inner wall → crank + studs from the inboard side → tube sleeves over the studs → belt → outer wall → hub over the double-D, hub sleeves → ring, nuts.
- **Yaw flange ↔ yaw tube** (rnd/parts/roll.py YAW_TIE): 6061-T6 flange (its hex spigot stays the torque path). 6 × M3 × 40 ISO 4762 class 12.9 go down from the tube's top end in steel crush sleeves Ø4.6 / Ø3.2 (ring → the flange's spigot top, 0.05 mm shorter than the print), heads on a steel clamp ring r 8.5–16.8 × 2 in a Ø34 × 5.5 counterbore (heads 0.5 mm under the top), through Ø3.4 holes in the wall into M3 threads tapped at the hex corners (r 11) of the flange's spigot + plate (8.3 mm engaged, Loctite 243); 1.2 kN each (≈ 0.5 N·m). Tightened from above on the bench, before the yaw block goes onto the roll output.
- Crush sleeves: turned 42CrMo4+QT (R_p0.2 ≥ 750 MPa) Ø7 / Ø4.3 (pitch, 8 pcs: 4 × the tube length, 4 × the hub) and Ø4.6 / Ø3.2 (yaw, 6 pcs), ends faced square, length = the measured print − 0.05 (ESTIMATE $3 each; E235 tube would yield at the bump and stall rows). The review's DIN 6796 disc springs (McMaster-Carr "DIN 6796 lock washers", norelem 07000, Bossard BN 794; load to flat M3 1.32 / M4 3.77 kN) were evaluated and not used: see the preload rows.
- Not drawn (rnd/parts/arm.py, arm track): the upper bone ↔ yaw flange screws. With the flange in aluminium they should be M4 into tapped holes in the flange, heads on washers on the bone flange, not inserts.

## C1: preload over life

φ = 2.0 design / 1.0 nominal (ESTIMATE, bounded from printed-PETG creep data: Aerospace 2022 9(3) 124, PMC12349189; Findley t^n + 1–2 decades of 40–50 °C shift); PETG α 68e-6/K (datasheet range 60–70e-6, ESTIMATE) vs steel 11.5e-6, assembled at 20 °C, coldest service 10 °C; embedding 10 µm per printed interface (ESTIMATE: FDM layer peaks; VDI 2230 gives ≈ 2–3 µm per machined metal interface, used for the metal joints).

- **pitch hub ↔ tube:** 4 × M4 10.9 at 1.50 kN in Ø7.0/4.3 steel crush sleeves (69.6 mm, 69 kN/mm; the print sandwiched with a 0.05 mm squeeze ≈ 1.3 MPa that may creep away): metal stack, embedding only → life preload **1.33 kN (88 %)** vs 0.72 kN for no gap under the worst service wrench (30.1 N·m, 0 N) → **1.85×**. Before: wave 3 as designed (print as the clamped member, 1.5 kN): bolt 43 vs print 183 µm/kN per bolt (69.6 mm of PETG: 274 µm of elastic squeeze, so the springs are bolt + print, not the bolt alone), life preload 0.46 kN (30 %; φ 1: 0.66 kN) vs 0.40 kN needed → 1.13×. Not chosen: the review's disc springs (3 × DIN 6796-M4 in series, 0.28 mm travel): life 0.71 kN but the softer bolts need 0.84 kN → 0.84× (the stiff bolts carried the bending). ✅
- **yaw flange ↔ tube:** 6 × M3 12.9 at 1.20 kN in Ø4.6/3.2 steel crush sleeves (29.7 mm, 58 kN/mm; the print sandwiched with a 0.05 mm squeeze ≈ 2.4 MPa that may creep away): metal stack, embedding only → life preload **1.05 kN (87 %)** vs 0.65 kN for no gap under the worst service wrench (32.6 N·m, 101 N) → **1.61×**. Before: wave 3 as designed (print as the clamped member, 1.0 kN): bolt 36 vs print 145 µm/kN per bolt (37.7 mm of PETG: 145 µm of elastic squeeze, so the springs are bolt + print, not the bolt alone), life preload 0.30 kN (30 %; φ 1: 0.43 kN) vs 0.34 kN needed → 0.86×. Not chosen: the review's disc springs (3 × DIN 6796-M3 in series, 0.53 mm travel): life 0.68 kN but the softer bolts need 0.69 kN → 0.99× (the stiff bolts carried the bending). ✅

# Hand-deflection compliance chain (generated by `python -m rnd.stiffness`)

The scorecard's hand sag (rnd/bones.py) only bends the carbon tubes. The joint encoders sit on the joint outputs, so
they see and correct belt stretch and KX twist, but not anything that bends or tilts **after** a joint output. This
chain adds those terms for the worst static case: 1 kg at the grasp point, arm straight out horizontally.

1. **Printed structure (FEA).** The four parts that carry the whole arm moment are re-solved with quadratic (P2)
   tetrahedra, which the review asked for (P1 tets are too stiff in bending), and with P1 on the same mesh for the
   ratio. Each part's loaded bearing seats are fitted with a rigid motion (translation t, rotation ω); the hand moves
   by t + ω × r (r = seat → hand). FEA loads are the ×1.5 design cases; the chain uses them ÷ 1.5.
2. **Bearing play.** A 61808 pair with C0 radial clearance (≈ 10 µm each, ESTIMATE) tilts by 2·c/span. Shimmed
   (light axial preload) pairs remove most of it: the chain uses 30 % of the free play for shimmed pairs.
3. **Carbon tubes** (rnd/bones.py), the CF segments only: bones.py also bends a printed "roll link" box (pitch → yaw)
   and a printed "elbow housing" box, which are the same parts step 1 already solves by FEA (counted twice until
   2026-11-27: 0.88 of its 1.85 mm).

Static case for the inline roll (the default drive; model correction 2026-11-27): the roll link and the yaw block get the
1 kg straight-out wrench itself instead of their ×1.5 strength cases ÷ 1.5. Pitch 90° with roll 0 puts the roll axis
along gravity, so the roll torque is 0 (the strength case also carries the drive's 35 N·m rated limit, ÷ 1.5 = 23 N·m,
at the same time), and the yaw torque is 0, so the yaw belt carries only its preload, which is there at zero payload
too (the strength case has the 691 N belt peak). The arm moment comes from the twin's point masses
(rnd/arm_sizing.point_masses): everything on the roll output about the roll axis for the roll link, everything hung
from the yaw shaft about the yaw seats' mid-level for the yaw block (the strength cases use 19 N·m ÷ 1.5 = 12.7 N·m for
both, which under-loads the roll link). The arm's ≈ 32 N shear at the yaw seats (< 6 % of the couple) is left out. The
bracket and the elbow housing keep their strength cases ÷ 1.5 (belt peak, a 3 kg forearm load: conservative).

The total is the static error a calibrated gravity model can largely remove (it is repeatable); the wrist camera closes
the loop for grasping in any case. Target R2b: uncompensated ≤ 6 mm, after the gravity model (assumed to remove 80 %) ≤ 2 mm.

**Static hand deflection, 1 kg straight out: 5.4 mm uncompensated (target ≤ 6), 1.1 mm after a gravity model (target ≤ 2).** ✅

## Cartridge flange ears: tipping and bolt load (Neon #2 finding 2)

Applied moment at the actuator peak = cartridge mass × 3 g × motor mid-length + Oldham side load (μ 0.2 · T / (D/3)) × the tenon height; tipping when it beats the ears' preload × their distance from the flange's edge line in the worst direction; preload 750 N per M4, and 30% of it after printed-joint creep (ESTIMATE). Friction torque μ 0.3 · n · F_p · r. Rule: ≥ 3 ears with no gap > 120°, or ≥ 4 with no gap > 180°. **D26 'now' rows (direct stages, no Oldham):** the side-load term is the motor bearing's share of the belt pull at the peak (cartridge_m.direct_brg_load) × its height over the flange (31 mm); the centring lip takes the shear. Lift 'now' is still the Oldham stage.
